name: Eric Campbell
period: New Guard and Centre Party leadership, 1931–1935; later fascist proposals take precedence within this period
description: Australian New Guard leader assessed through anti-communist mobilisation and his later proposals for a corporative state.

religion.reason: A Presbyterian funeral in 1970 does not firmly establish personal religious identification during 1931–1935; membership policy was not a personal profession.

sources.title: Eric Campbell (political activist) — biography and positions
Campbell, Eric (1893–1970)
sources.publisher: Australian National University / Australian Dictionary of Biography

sources.title: Australian anti-communists and the lure of the United States

axes.brief: Paramilitary opposition to Lang developed into proposals for corporative authoritarian government.
axes.counterEvidence: Participation in the 1935 election and constitutionalist claims qualify, but do not erase, authoritarian proposals.

axes.brief: Anti-communist mobilisation and organised political force favour coercion against perceived subversion.
axes.counterEvidence: His movement’s own protests do not demonstrate a universal right for opposing disruptive assemblies.

axes.brief: British imperial loyalty and national unity guide his political activity.
axes.counterEvidence: The New Guard claimed recruitment regardless of religious creed; cultural nationalism is not proof of every racial-biology claim.

qualifications.15: The statement specifically includes several distinct ways of life within national identity; it does not ask whether a common national identity should exist.

axes.brief: Imperial loyalty and customary community preservation favour selective entry.
axes.counterEvidence: No personal detailed visa programme was established; general interwar Australian law is contextual, not his recorded answer.

qualifications.5: The statement permits permanent refugee settlement regardless of skills or cultural compatibility. The answer concerns this unconditional clause, separately from selected humanitarian admissions.

axes.brief: Military experience and paramilitary organisation favour preparedness and coercive capacity.
axes.counterEvidence: Domestic activity is not evidence of a specific expeditionary-war programme.

axes.brief: National authority is understood within British imperial loyalty rather than general foreign political control.
axes.counterEvidence: Imperial allegiance qualifies purely Australian sovereignty; modern global institutions are analogies.

axes.brief: Anti-communism protects private enterprise and property within later corporative supervision.
axes.counterEvidence: Opposing socialism does not require privatising every railway or public utility.

axes.brief: Domestic business and imperial preference suggest guarded rather than wholly unrestricted commerce.
axes.counterEvidence: The dossier does not establish a complete personal tariff programme; ideological labels cannot supply one.

axes.brief: His later corporative proposals qualify earlier defence of free private business.
axes.counterEvidence: Collective economic organisation differs from state ownership and comprehensive assigned production.

axes.brief: Protection of business and property favours limited social provision over compulsory equalisation.
axes.counterEvidence: Veteran solidarity and service obligations permit welfare; opposition to Lang is not a tax-by-tax personal manifesto.

axes.brief: Civic imperial loyalty and religiously open membership do not establish a clerical state.
axes.counterEvidence: Christian cultural convention may remain; his eventual funeral is outside the assessed period.

axes.brief: Established national and family conventions are more likely than radical social liberalisation.
axes.counterEvidence: A reactionary political programme does not directly document every modern sexual and gender-law mechanism.

axes.brief: Technical and military modernisation can coexist with social caution and inherited institutions.
axes.counterEvidence: Contemporary biomedical mechanisms remain analogies; military experience is not unconditional technological permissiveness.

axes.brief: Central corporative leadership and coercive national unity limit regional autonomy.
axes.counterEvidence: Activity in New South Wales does not itself demonstrate federal decentralism.

axes.brief: Imperial cultural formation coexists with conventional views of sex roles and character.
axes.counterEvidence: Neither nationality nor anti-communism proves genetic group differences; causal estimates remain weak.
